data.title: Hričov Castle in 3D – a castle on an almost impregnable crag
data.excerpt: The ruin of Hričov Castle rises on a prominent crag of the Súľovské skály, an almost impregnable site protected for the most part by high, steep rock faces. Together with Mária Takáčová we have attempted a 3D visualisation of the castle, which was built in the 13th century on the site of an earlier, probably timber hillfort and was finally plundered and destroyed by the soldiers of Stephen Bocskai.

mediaTexts.alt: A 3D reconstruction of a stone castle on a rocky crag, with spruces in the foreground

children.text: The ruin of Hričov Castle rises on a prominent rocky crag that is visible even from the motorway leading from Považská Bystrica to Žilina. The castle crag is one of the spurs of the Súľovské skály, and it created an almost impregnable site, protected for the most part by high and steep rock faces that presented attackers with a problem hard to solve. The name Hričov derives from the word Grič (meaning hill, rock, rocky). The word grič has the same meaning in Serbo-Croatian as well. In Slovakia this word occurs from the earliest times. It was used as a place name in the first written mention, in the form “castrum Hrichov” (1265; more precisely, this charter refers back to 1254).

The castle crag was already occupied in the period of the Púchov culture and later apparently by the Slavs as well, as is shown above all by finds of pottery from these periods. The stone castle on the site of an earlier, apparently timber hillfort arose apparently in the 13th century, and historians assume that, as one of the few Hungarian castles, it was built still before the Mongol invasion of 1241/1242. In 1265 the above-mentioned donation charter of Béla IV is already recorded, in which he granted the castle to Mikuláš, son of Pavol of the Bejč family. Later the castle was acquired by the Balaša family, during whose ownership it came into the power of Matúš Čák of Trenčín. After Matúš’s death the castle returned for a short time to the Balaša family, only for the king to acquire it again in the second half of the 14th century.

He had the original castle fundamentally rebuilt, when a bailey with a bastion was added to the palace rising on the highest part of the rocky crag. King Sigismund of Luxembourg granted the castle to his wife Barbara, who had it repaired. Subsequently, however, it fell into the hands of the Hussite captain Mikuláš Švidrigal. Later the castle was recaptured, and in a later period King Matthias Corvinus granted it to Blažej Podmanický. His descendant, the well-known robber knight Rafael Podmanický, waged armed struggles over the castle, but also a “struggle” in the legal field, which finally led to his managing to prove, on the basis of archival charters, that the castle belonged to the Podmanický family.

It was apparently in this period that the palace buildings were erected in the area of the bailey, and a narrow corridor cut into the rock and terminated by a tower also came into being, which provided good protection for the access road to the castle. After the said building-up of the original bailey, a new bailey arose on the level ground in front of the gate. This was apparently protected by a timber palisade. The said period represents the time of the castle’s greatest flourishing. Later, in the 17th century, when the castle became the property of the Thurzo family, it gradually began to decline and the centre of the estate was moved to Bytča. The definitive end of the castle was brought about by the soldiers of Stephen Bocskai, who plundered and destroyed it.

We carried out the attempt at a visualisation presented here in cooperation with Mária Takáčová, a student of Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra. Unfortunately we had no lidar data available, so take the terrain model as approximate. The structure itself corresponds to the ground plan of the castle, and the details are worked out according to the archaeological insights from the excavation of the castle.
